## A Game-Based Intervention Promotes Social-Cognitive Development in Early Childhood in

Brazilian Urban Poverty Contexts

Abstract: Adversities experienced during early childhood can have powerful and long-lasting

influences that may affect the development of cognitive, social, and emotional skills. Game-based

interventions, played by groups of peers and focused on optimizing social cognition, may address

these effects and improve resilience, positively impacting academic achievement and social well-

being. However, empirical evidence for the effectiveness of such interventions remains limited,

particularly in low- and middle-income countries where their impact may be especially beneficial.

In this study, we developed and preliminarily evaluated a game-based curriculum designed to

enhance children’s understanding of social and emotional information, critical skills for effective

communication, metacognition, and learning from others. In a preregistered, double-blind cluster-

randomized pilot study conducted in Brazil, we evaluated the effectiveness of the Social Game-

Based Intervention, CuriousMind, in the context of urban poverty among preschool children.

Schools were randomized to one of three conditions: CuriousMind, a game-based math

intervention (active control), or a no-treatment control. Children were evaluated before and after

the 10-week intervention. CuriousMind significantly enhanced children’s social and emotional

skills, particularly in emotion labeling, emotion recognition, and emotion situation knowledge,

providing evidence that game-based interventions with peers can effectively promote social-

cognitive development in early childhood.

Key-words: social cognition, early childhood, game; intervention, resilience.

## 1. Introduction

Early childhood is a sensitive period for human neurodevelopment, during which

fundamental cognitive, social, and emotional skills emerge and mature. Adversities experienced

during this period can have powerful and long-lasting influences1. Social determinants of health,

such as adversity associated with poverty, social isolation, exposure to violence, and lack of peer

or family support, are also associated with social, emotional, and cognitive difficulties, with

impacts on learning that lead to gaps in long-term achievement and quality of life2,3,4. Furthermore,

research in social and cognitive neuroscience reveals that poverty affects the brain bases of

cognitive, social, and emotional development in ways that can compromise future learning2,5,6,7,8.

Early intervention is key to preventing the emergence or progression of developmental

problems. Programs targeting early childhood show larger effects compared with interventions

targeting subsequent stages of development9. The preschool period, in particular, is central to

developing skills that engender the acquisition of formal knowledge later at school10,11. Thus,

intervening during the preschool years has the potential to prevent developmental delays and to

promote cognitive skills and mental health, especially for children in socially and economically

disadvantaged contexts.

Human social abilities are rooted in the propensity to engage with others, learn from them,

and use acquired social information in the complex interactions that make up our daily activities.

Referred to as ‘social cognition,’ these abilities are critical for effective communication,

metacognition, and learning12, the basis of which emerges as early as infancy and follows a

progressive developmental trajectory throughout the early childhood period and beyond13. Social

cognition also supports children’s “learning to learn”, that is, their ability to assess what they know

and do not know, to understand the pedagogical communications of teachers and other adults, to

provide others with relevant information, to cooperate with others in performing group tasks, and

to regulate their attention and emotions to foster a supportive group-learning environment14,15. In

particular, research in developmental cognitive science provides evidence that preschool children

universally develop intuitive abilities to understand people’s intentions and beliefs, emotions,

social relationships, feelings, and actions, often referred to as theory of mind16-23.

Interventions in socio-cognitive domains during early childhood have the potential to

enhance these skills directly and may have secondary beneficial effects on resilience and academic

achievement9. Beauchamp and Anderson24, for example, underscore this critical role of social

cognition, emphasizing its interaction with executive functions to facilitate the development of

social skills. Previous research also establishes an evidence base for programs designed to enhance

social and emotional skills, with findings highlighting significant improvements in emotion

recognition25, emotion regulation and stress management9,25,26, social competence, problem-

solving skills, empathy, prosocial behavior,9,25,26, and self-efficacy and decision-making skills9.

Some studies also report that such programs increase the frequency of positive emotions and

decrease the frequency of negative expressions as evaluated by teachers25,26, as well as reduce

Finally, such programs have contributed to increased involvement in classroom activities,

enhanced academic performance9,27, and better economic and vocational outcomes in adulthood10.

Building on this evidence base, universal school-based programs targeting socio-cognitive

and emotional skills are increasingly recognized as a cost-effective and scalable approach capable

of operating as a population-level strategy to strengthen mental health and well-being, as well as

potentially increasing involvement in classroom activities and enhancing academic performance

within educational contexts28.  Despite these documented benefits, important limitations remain.

A central limitation is that few interventions are designed to account for ecological, cultural, and

institutional realities9. Furthermore, prior research frequently does not encompass empirical

evidence that remains limited in low- and middle-income countries, particularly with respect to

game-based interventions in early childhood.

Game-based interventions differ from traditional teaching methods in terms of

engagement, motivation, and learning outcomes29. Game-based methodology enhances experience

and increases motivation and engagement, eliciting positive emotions and skill development,

especially in childhood30. Consistent with this premise, a recent meta-analysis synthesizing 136

game-based interventions published between 2013 and 2023 (total N = 1,426) suggested that such

interventions lead to improvements in social skills, empathy, cooperation, reductions in aggressive

behavior, and broader social-emotional competencies, including self-regulation and teacher–child

interaction31.

Although play is ubiquitous in early childhood, access to validated game-based curricula

remains limited. When available, such programs are rarely adapted to local community

characteristics and cultural contexts, and often fail to incorporate stimuli that are ecologically valid

and developmentally engaging. To foster environments that are both positive and meaningful,

particularly in vulnerable populations, interventions must be empirically grounded while

remaining contextually attuned. Despite the documented promise of game-based approaches, few

curricula focusing on social cognition have undergone such rigorous validation, especially in low-

and middle-income countries, where contextual demands and implementation constraints are most

pronounced 9.

culturally adaptable framework, we previously examined whether such approaches could enhance

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Participants and Setting

Sample size determination was guided by an a priori statistical power analysis conducted

using G*Power (version 3.1) for detecting a group × time interaction in a repeated-measures

design. The analysis was based on an F test for a repeated-measures ANOVA with a within–

between interaction, assuming three groups (control, math intervention, and social intervention)

and two measurement occasions (pre- and post-intervention). A medium effect size was specified

(Cohen’s f = 0.30), with the significance level set at α = .05 and desired statistical power of .80.

Under these assumptions, the analysis indicated that a total sample size of 111 participants would

be required to detect the target interaction effect. In the present study, data were collected from

118 participants, 107 of whom provided complete and valid data for analysis.

Participants included 5- and 6-year-old children (M = 69.7 months, SD = 4.45, range = 60-

82 months; n = 50 girls, n = 57 boys) who enrolled in the final year of preschool. In Brazil, school

entry follows a March cutoff and the academic year runs from February to December; because

data collection occurred in the second semester, children in this cohort were older, accounting for

the observed mean age and range. The sample comprised 35 children in the CuriousMind group,

34 in the active control, and 38 in the no-treatment control. We found no evidence of baseline

differences across groups in age (F[2, 103]= 2.46, p=0.090) or gender (χ2 = 1.17, p=0.557, see

*Table 1). All children were from families with low socioeconomic status (SES), with 83.3% of the*

sample living at or below the poverty line, as defined by the World Bank35. None of the children’s

mothers had a university degree, only 37.5% had completed high school, and 4.2% were illiterate.

Children were recruited from six public preschools located in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil and had to

be enrolled and 60–83 months-of-age to participate. Child gender was reported by parents or legal

guardians using a structured sociodemographic questionnaire administered at baseline. Children

were excluded from the analyses if they had a reported diagnosis of a neurological or

neurodevelopmental disorder (e.g., Autism Spectrum Disorder), a severe sensory impairment (e.g.,

blindness), or had withdrawn from school before the post-intervention assessment. Participants

and their families did not receive any financial or material compensation for participation in the

### 2.2 Study Design and Procedures

The study employed a small-scale, classroom-based, cluster-randomized, double-blind,

parallel three-arm trial design (allocation ratio 1:1:1) at the school level. Six preschools located in

low-income urban areas of Brazil participated, with two different preschools randomly assigned

to each experimental condition: (a) CuriousMind, (b) math games (active control, adapted from

Dillon et al.32), and (c) a no-treatment control group. The math games, active control condition

was included to ensure that any benefits of the social-cognitive games stemmed from their social

and emotional content rather than from the general rules and procedures common to both sets of

games.

Randomization was performed at the cluster level using the Sealed Envelope online

randomization tool (https://www.sealedenvelope.com/simple-randomiser/v1/lists), which

generated a concealed allocation sequence until implementation. Because the intervention was

administered to all the children in each classroom, randomization occurred at the classroom level,

not at the participant level. All primary analyses were conducted at the individual level but are

thus interpreted as preliminary given the limited number of clusters and the exploratory nature of

the trial.

The study followed rigorous double-blind procedures. The intervention and evaluation

teams operated entirely independently: Research assistants responsible for classroom

implementation had no involvement in assessment activities, and assessors collecting outcome

data were blind to group allocation throughout the study. Teachers and research assistants

implementing the interventions were unaware of the study hypotheses and were not informed about

the content or aims of the other experimental conditions.

### 2.3 The Game-Based Intervention Protocol

CuriousMind

Our social-game curriculum, CuriousMind, was designed to be scalable and easy to

implement. It consisted of two games: ‘Emotion Explorer’ and ‘Mind Hunter’ (see Figure1). The

games were designed for group play using concrete, non-digital materials that were simultaneously

visible to all children, with turn-taking required throughout the activity. The games featured

characters that represented a diverse range of genders, ethnicities, races, and individuals with

disabilities.

Emotion Explorer is an untimed board game that exercises intuitive concepts of emotion,

as well as the actions, states, and events that elicit emotional expressions. The game has 10 levels

that increase in difficulty and complexity according to a progression that complements social-

emotional development35. The game includes emotion recognition of primary, secondary, and

mixed emotions and emotional situation knowledge through cartoons and story-based narratives

describing situations that tend to elicit specific emotions. The initial phase focuses on emotion

recognition through photographs of facial expressions, whereas the following phases involve

interpreting emotions depicted in cartoon scenarios and story-based situations. (See

Supplementary Figure 2 for procedural details.) These situations were identified through a co-

design methodology, employing semi-structured questionnaires and a focus group with five

experienced early childhood education teachers and psychologists specializing in

neurodevelopment, with all members of the focus group from the local context. The teachers

provided critical insights into the social interactions and scenarios most relevant for children in the

target group, the psychologists ensured the developmental appropriateness of the selected

situations, and the researchers acted as facilitators. This approach combined practitioner expertise

with theoretical knowledge, enabling the development of collaboratively generated, contextually

meaningful, and developmentally appropriate game content36.

In the initial game dynamics, children play in pairs on a shared board containing six spaces

(three on each side) and alternate turns. In the following game dynamic, the teacher conducts a

group activity by reading short stories about the game characters. Each child uses an individual

board with four spaces and marks (with a marker or pen) the emotion corresponding to the

character’s feeling in each story.

For Emotion Explorer, facial-expression stimuli used across both phases of the game were

selected from three validated facial-expression stimulus sets available for scientific research use:

the Radboud Faces Database37, the NIMH Child Emotional Faces Picture Set (NIMH-ChEFS38),

and the Child Affective Facial Expression Set (CAFE39). The use of these stimuli followed the

access and use conditions specified by each database. Illustrations, graphic elements, and game-

Mind Hunter is a card game that aims to exercise intuitive concepts of the relations among

perception, desires, beliefs, and intentional action that emerge in infancy40,41. Each round consists

of 16 cards played in groups of four children. The game has eight levels with increasing difficulty

and complexity based on the development of theory of mind such that four different mental-state

contrasts are included: diverse desire, diverse belief, knowledge access, and first- and second-order

false belief22. All scenarios are presented through drawn illustrations without written text,

emphasizing visual-perceptual cues rather than linguistic mediation. Players interpret scenarios

depicting the main character’s mental state and select the most congruent outcome from two

options, one outlined in blue and the other in red (See Supplementary Figure 3 for more details).

The player places the card in the box of the corresponding color of the congruent option and then

passes it to the next child, who responds to that card. The sequence continues until all four children

have completed the level.

For Mind Hunter, visual stimuli were sourced from Flaticon (www.flaticon.com) under the

applicable Flaticon license. Target images were identified using English-language search terms,

downloaded in PNG format, and incorporated into the game cards. The cards were assembled using

Adobe PowerPoint and Adobe Photoshop. All additional illustrations, layout, and game-design

elements were created by the study design team.

Math Games Intervention (active control)

Detailed information on the full Math Games Intervention (active control) is provided in

prior work32. In the present study, this condition consisted of two group-based games, Find and

Move and Find the Shape. The social and math games were methodologically aligned so that the

math games could serve as an active control condition, with equivalent pedagogical principles and

cognitive demands across both curricula. This design ensured equivalent opportunities for all

children to engage with the tasks and contribute responses, supporting reliable individual-level

estimates of performance given the sample size.

Find and Move is an untimed board game with eight decks of cards that, similar to

Emotion Explorer, follows a structured sequence of levels increasing in difficulty and complexity.

The game targets core numerical cognition skills, including comparison of magnitudes, counting,

addition, and compositional operations based on the base-ten structure of the number system.

Children play in pairs, alternating turns and engaging cooperatively to solve each numerical

challenge, mirroring the social dynamics of the emotion game. Each card displays a numerical

Find the Shape: is an untimed card game designed to enhance sensitivity to geometric

forms, their parts, and their properties. The game, structurally parallel to Mind Hunter, follows a

progressive format with 10 decks of 16 cards each, played across eight sessions by groups of four

children. Children determine which of two shapes shares a specific geometric property, presented

using either non-symbolic or symbolic information. Each round presents a visual clue at the top of

the card, such as the number of sides, the equality of angles, or the presence of parallel lines, that

guides children in identifying the correct option between two choices, one outlined in blue and the

other in red. As in Mind Hunter, children take alternating turns, placing their chosen cards into the

corresponding colored box before passing the deck to the next player. With progressively

increasing levels of difficulty, children identify similar shapes using the clues provided to guide

their choices. This game aims to stimulate both intuitive and formal knowledge related to the

recognition and discrimination of geometric shapes and their properties.

### 2.4 Teacher Training and Implementation Fidelity

Teachers received training from the research team for the implementation of both sets of

games. Training sessions were conducted separately for each condition, totaling 12 hours of

instruction before the programs’ implementation. This training was followed by weekly meetings

with trained researchers to clarify methodological procedures once the intervention began.

During the intervention, children played their assigned games in the classroom with their

teacher and a trained research assistant. The implementation monitoring team conducted

unannounced classroom observations to assess intervention fidelity. Their visits were scheduled

according to the weekly session timetables provided by the teachers, although teachers were not

informed of the specific day any visit would occur. Monitoring data were collected using electronic

### 2.5. Outcome Measures and Pre-/Post-Intervention Assessments

Assessments evaluating the effects of the intervention were administered at two time

points: during the month prior to the intervention (pre-test) and during the month following the

intervention (post-test). Children were tested individually on a laptop computer by a trained

research assistant blind to the intervention condition. To determine pre- and post-intervention

social-cognitive abilities, each child completed two different versions of a comprehensive social-

assessment battery, including five tasks. Based on Dillon et al.32, the two versions featured items

that were matched for content and difficulty. Given their important link to social-cognitive

development24, executive functions were also assessed. Mathematics assessments were also

administered as part of the preregistered study protocol; however, analyses of these measures fall

outside the scope of the present work.

Emotion Discrimination

Six faces are presented on a computer screen, five of which represent the same emotion,

while the “intruder” expresses a different emotion. The stimuli are drawn from the Radboud and

NIMH face stimulus sets37,38. The experimenter asks the child to “Point to the person who looks

like they’re feeling something different from everybody else.” Participants are thus asked to

identify the “emotion intruder” for each one of the nine trials.

Emotion Recognition (Point to Emotion Task).

In each of nine trials, children see six faces showing distinct emotions and are asked to

point to the face expressing the emotion named by the experimenter (e.g., “Show me who feels

happy”). Stimuli were drawn from the Radboud and NIMH face sets37,38. This task measures

children’s ability to recognize and discriminate basic emotions.

Emotion Labeling (Say the Emotion Task).

In each of eight trials, a single face is presented, and children are asked to verbally name

the emotion depicted. This task assesses emotion knowledge and expressive vocabulary.

Social Situations Emotion Knowledge

The experimenter verbally presents brief oral social scenarios, based on the Emotion

Matching Task (EMT)42, to the participant. These scenarios involve one or more characters and

Theory of Mind

The theory of mind test used 18-items featuring theory of mind scenarios that cover the

main subdomains of this interconnected set of sensitivities24: diverse desires, diverse beliefs,

knowledge access, false belief, hidden emotion, and agents’ intentions. The scenarios encompass

six of the seven categories of mental states highlighted by Beaudoin et al.14. Presented with pictures

or verbal descriptions, the child is asked to deduce different agents’ mental states. Examples of the

trials include items based on the Sally-Anne paradigm45, on access to knowledge and agent’s action

(adapted from Baker et al.18) or based on agent’s preference considering the amount of effort an

agent expended in order to reach a target/goal (adapted from Jara-Ettinger et al.18,46).

Utility Calculus (Park Play Task)

Children are presented with short narratives accompanying pictures describing an agent in

a park or zoo who wants to visit different attractions. In each story, although three attractions were

possible in principle, only two were open on that day, and the agent was unaware of which two

were available. After each of four stories like this, children are asked to identify the agent’s

preferred attraction. In the park trials, the agent expressed disappointment as a socio-cognitive cue,

whereas no emotional cues were provided in the zoo trials. The task was adapted from Baker et

al17.

Executive Functions

Executive functions were assessed using an inhibition and cognitive flexibility task

previously validated in the Brazilian population47. The task consists of 72 trials across four

conditions presented in a fixed order: 1) naming animals (baseline trials, 12 trials); 2) naming

animals whose heads are occluded but bodies are visible (control trials, 12 trials); 3) naming

animals whose body is displayed with the head of another animal (conflict trials, 24 trials); 4)

### 2.6 Statistical Analyses

A score for each assessment was calculated as the percentage of correct responses (the

number of correct trials divided by the total number of administered trials), excluding practice

trials. Responses categorized as “I don’t know” or “refuse to answer” were coded as incorrect. Z-

scores were calculated for each test by standardizing the percentage of correct responses to the

pretest baseline scores of the no-treatment control group.

A social composite score was calculated as the main dependent variable as the average of

the Z-scores for percentage correct performance across the social-cognitive tasks (Emotion

Discrimination, Emotion Recognition, Emotion Labeling, Social Situations Emotion Knowledge,

and Theory of Mind). Reliability and dimensionality analyses are reported in the Supplementary

Methods.

Analyses were performed in R48. Assumptions of parametric statistics were examined to

ensure the validity of subsequent analyses. Since all variables were standardized (Z-scores) prior

to analysis, parameter estimates are expressed in standard deviation units corresponding to

standardized effect sizes. Parameters indicated acceptable distributions for all outcome measures.

Analyses were based on a regression specification, that was preregistered on April 21, 2020, along

with a complete pre-analysis plan available at https://osf.io/npyvw/files/xynrk. Although the pre-

analysis plan was registered after the study was conducted, it was finalized prior to any data

analysis, and all analyses were performed only after preregistration. We used the following

regression framework:

y ~ social + math + baseline + error (1)

Where “y” represents the posttest score of an outcome measure, “social” is a dummy-coded

indicator variable for whether a child was in the CuriousMind condition, “math” is a dummy-coded

indicator variable for whether a child was in the math games condition, and “baseline” is the

baseline performance on an outcome measure. The error term was not clustered at the class level

because with only two classes per treatment condition, there was insufficient power to detect a

treatment effect at that level. Thus, our analysis did not account for correlations in performance

within each classroom, and the results of our analyses are regarded as preliminary. No a priori

## 3. Results

Based on the information gathered by teachers and process monitors during gameplay,

initial evaluations were conducted to determine if the two game-based interventions were

effectively implemented and captivated the children’s interest. Both CuriousMind and the math

games were consistently played, with a high level of participation observed. In the preschools

where these games were conducted, every child was engaged in the games during 71.5% and

81.5% of the sessions for CuriousMind and the math games.

At post-test, children in the CuriousMind condition showed gains that were 0.65 standard

deviations (SD) higher on the social composite, 1.26 SDs higher on emotion recognition, 1.27 SDs

higher on emotion labeling, and 0.39 SDs higher on emotion situation knowledge. By contrast,

children in the math games condition and no-treatment control groups showed no comparable

progress on social-cognitive measures: Their social composite scores remained largely stable, and

in some cases declined (Table 2). Children who participated in the CuriousMind condition

demonstrated higher post-test accuracy on social-cognitive measures than those in either control

## 4. Discussion

This small-scale, randomized double-blind trial was conducted in Salvador-Bahia, Brazil,

to evaluate the impact of CuriousMind, a game-based intervention training social-cognitive

abilities, which targeted preschool children from low SES backgrounds. Compared with children

in both active and a no-treatment control groups, children in the CuriousMind group, who engaged

in 60 hours of immersive gameplay in their regular classrooms, demonstrated marked

improvements in social-cognitive abilities.

CuriousMind included two games, Emotion Explorer, a board game focusing on emotion

recognition and labeling, and Mind Hunter, a card game focusing on theory of mind. Consistent

with the games’ content, children in the CuriousMind condition showed marked improvements in

their labeling and recognition of emotions, as well as in their understanding of the causes and

consequences of emotions. Such gains are consistent with previous research suggesting that

interactive and structured play can be a potent tool in early childhood education for boosting social

and emotional learning27 and further show that these games in particular can effectively augment

specific social-cognitive skills.

Despite children’s substantial improvements in the overall social composite score, as well

as in specific domains directly targeted by the intervention, no significant improvements were

observed in children’s theory of mind or emotion discrimination. While the games effectively

targeted specific areas of social cognition, their impact thus did not transfer to all social cognitive

domains, consistent with findings that cognitive interventions often yield improvements specific

to the content and tasks they train14.

The findings nevertheless contribute to the growing evidence that playful, directed

interventions can effectively nurture social and emotional development in early-childhood-

education settings, even amidst adverse socio-economic conditions49,50. Game-based materials

leverage children’s natural affinity for play, significantly boosting their engagement and

motivation, which is crucial for deep and meaningful learning experiences32. CuriousMind, in

particular, demonstrates significant promise and aligns with the literature suggesting that game-

based approaches are beneficial for enhancing social and emotional abilities, preventing, and

mitigating mental health disorders, and potentially positively impacting academic outcomes49,51,52.

The practical applications of social-cognitive game interventions, especially in diverse and

sometimes adverse environments, highlights the robustness and adaptability of the methods

employed. Such interventions not only aim to develop cognitive skills but also focus extensively

on the emotional and social growth of children, which are critical to their overall development and

future educational success. The significance of integrating emotional and social learning into early

childhood education curricula is supported by a substantial body of research that underscores the

interconnectedness of emotional competence and academic performance 9, 51.

Finally, early interventions, specifically those that are playful and directed towards

developing social cognition, offer a proactive approach to addressing the broader spectrum of

children’s developmental needs. Collectively, game-based, social-cognitive, and early approaches

not only lay a foundation for academic success but also cultivate essential social skills and

emotional intelligence, equipping individuals to thrive in complex social environments32, 33, 34, 53.

The successful implementation of CuriousMind provides a template for future educational

programs aimed at fostering a holistic educational experience. This aligns with the growing

advocacy for education systems to incorporate comprehensive educational strategies that consider

social-emotional development as central to both learning and well-being11,56.

Overall, the present findings underscore the potential of the CuriousMind intervention as a

model for culturally grounded and developmentally appropriate pedagogical approaches, with

scope for scalability and integration into everyday educational settings. Such frameworks may

enhance the effectiveness of educational interventions designed to influence dynamic, real-world

conditions54 across diverse demographic contexts, particularly within social-cognitive

domains49,55,56. The lessons learned here underline the importance of interdisciplinary

### 4.1. Limitations

While the study contributes significantly to the existing literature, some limitations warrant

acknowledgment. The relatively small sample size and the specificity of the geographical and

cultural context call for broader and more diverse sampling in future research to strengthen

generalizability. In addition, the presence of baseline differences between groups necessitates

cautious interpretation of the observed changes over time. Although the analytical models

accounted for clustering and initial performance levels, and additional cluster-robust sensitivity

analyses yielded consistent estimates, residual baseline imbalance cannot be entirely ruled out as

a contributing factor to the magnitude of change detected. Accordingly, the observed reversal from

lower baseline performance to higher post-intervention performance should be interpreted as

evidence of differential developmental trajectories associated with the intervention, rather than as

conclusive group superiority at a single assessment point. In light of the clustered design, initial

non-equivalence, pilot nature of the trial and the limited number of clusters, these findings should

nevertheless be interpreted as preliminary and warrant replication in larger and fully balanced

samples, although they provide promising initial evidence regarding the direction and relative

magnitude of intervention effects. Furthermore, the absence of improvement in certain domains,

such as theory of mind, suggests that further refinement in game design and complementary

instructional strategies may be required to more effectively facilitate near-transfer to complex

socio-emotional skills in diverse settings.

## 5. Conclusion

The rigorous, field-based test of CuriousMind highlights the potential of game-based

learning to enhance the social-cognitive skills of young children, particularly in cultivating specific

social and emotional abilities in preschool children from low SES backgrounds. While the results

are promising, they underscore the need for continued research focused on an in-depth

understanding of the development of social cognition in early childhood across diverse contexts

and on the importance of validated measures. The role of CuriousMind in enhancing children’s

social-cognitive skills nevertheless lays the groundwork for future large-scale randomized

# Falling for cardiac output: an enticing new orthostatic phenotype

**Authors:** Aldis H. Petriceks; Grace R. Lee; Stephen P. Juraschek

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Division of General Medicine, 330 Brookline Avenue, Boston, MA 02215, USA; | 2Harvard Medical School, Boston MA, USA

## Abstract

Humans transition frequently from the supine or seated position to standing. This fundamental activity is functionally imperceptible when supported by intact cardiovascular and autonomic responses. Both global and specific impairments in the cardiovascular and autonomic systems can lead to debilitating orthostatic intolerance syndromes. Unfortunately, orthostatic signs and symptoms do not regularly point to the specific pathological pathway responsible for orthostatic intolerance, making treatment challenging for clinicians.

Improved management of orthostatic intolerance syndromes requires deeper knowledge of the underlying pathways responsible for their presentation. In their study published in this issue of the European Heart Journal, Xie and colleagues focus on an important and understudied parameter central to orthostatic transitions: cardiac output (CO).1 Their rigorous, detailed, and large population study suggests new directions for orthostatic research and management.

Among healthy individuals, orthostatic haemodynamic regulation is complex. Immediately after standing from the supine position, blood pools in lower extremity veins due to gravity.2 This decreases venous return to the heart, leading to decreased pre-load and cardiac stroke volume (SV). Cardiac output is a function of SV and heart rate (HR), and therefore decreases as a result. The peripheral arterial vasculature also relaxes initially, reducing systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Because mean arterial pressure (MAP) is a function of CO and SVR, blood pressure (BP) decreases initially upon standing.3,4 However, the autonomic and cardiovascular systems compensate for this decreased BP immediately. Baroreceptors in the carotid vessels and right atrium detect decreased arterial pressure and trigger increased sympathetic activity. In turn, HR increases (through beta-adrenergic activity) and contraction of lower extremity and abdominal skeletal muscle mobilizes venous blood to the central circulation, increasing preload and SV. This leads to increased CO and MAP. In addition, SVR increases due to smooth muscle contraction in the arterial system (alpha-adrenergic response), further increasing MAP. As a result, BP typically normalizes within 30 s after standing.5

In their work, Xie et al. characterized the CO response to orthostatic challenge.1 They aimed to identify novel phenotypes of CO during and after standing among older and younger adults along with their causes and clinical implications. To achieve these aims, the authors used non-invasive, continuous haemodynamic monitoring during supine-to-standing protocols in two cohorts. The first cohort included 3074 young adults from Melbourne, Australia, without history of cardiovascular or neurological disease. This study did not have clinical outcomes data. The second cohort included 3025 older adults from The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA), age 50 years or older in Ireland. Clinical outcomes (e.g. falls, frailty, and cognition) were reported in the year prior to or since the preceding visit. In both cohorts, the authors examined sympathetic vascular tone and baroreflex sensitivity. To investigate the mechanisms behind CO phenotypes, participants in the Melbourne cohort specifically underwent haemodynamic monitoring with vasodilatory (using sublingual nitroglycerine) and vasoconstrictive (using active handgrip and intravenous phenylephrine) interventions.

Participants fell into one of two CO phenotypes. Among one group, CO increased immediately after standing and remained elevated (COR), demonstrating increased HR and appropriate recovery of SVR. In the second phenotype, after an initial rise in CO, CO subsequently decreased (COF), with a smaller increase in HR compared with COR. Only a minority of individuals with COF also had orthostatic hypotension (OH). COF was observed in both older and younger cohorts. Moreover, in TILDA, COF was associated with increased falls, frailty, and lower functional and cognitive performance. Negative chronotropic agents strengthened the association between COF and fall events, and COF participants taking negative chronotropic agents had a lower increase in HR than COR participants. Contrary to expectation, COF was more prevalent in the younger cohort; however, the clinical significance of COF among the younger cohort was not clear from available data.

The authors report that COF reflects ‘a dissociation between autonomic activation and its vascular and cardiac effects.’ However, multiple explanations exist about the underlying physiology of this phenotype. For instance, the decreased SV in the COF group may reflect inadequate cardiac response to increased beta-adrenergic activity. On the other hand, decreased SV could be due to increased pooling of blood in lower extremity and abdominal veins, dampening venous return. Multiple explanations also exist for the finding of ‘blunted’ HR augmentation in the COF phenotypes. Contrary to expectation, this could in fact suggest a robust, compensatory systemic vascular response to standing, similar to reflex bradycardia observed in patients treated with the vasopressor phenylephrine. Blunted HR augmentation could also indicate a hypoactive beta-adrenergic response to standing, at either the autonomic or the cardiomyocyte level.

The increased prevalence of COF in young participants is hard to interpret without clinical outcomes data, and could convey a distinct phenotype compared with older adults. The authors speculate that younger people have greater venous compliance than older adults, which may cause increased orthostatic venous pooling and decreased SV. In this case, COF might not be clinically concerning for most young people. It is also possible that a robust vasoconstrictive response in younger people could itself obviate the need for CO augmentation. The authors suggest that increased basal sympathetic activity in older adults could partly explain the lower COF prevalence in this cohort. However, if COF is (at least in some cases) due to ‘a dissociation between autonomic activation and its vascular and cardiac effects’, it is unclear to what extent this increased sympathetic input should mitigate age-related cardiovascular changes.

COF may also be on the spectrum of pathophysiology related to vasovagal effects such as the Bezold–Jarisch reflex, characterized by both HR blunting and arterial vasodilation. In severe cases, these two pathological responses may result in vasovagal or neurocardiogenic syncope due to hypotension and loss of consciousness.6,7 Though vasovagal effects were not a focus of the present study and not observed, interpersonal variation in vasovagal input (without syncope) could explain some degree of the COF phenotype captured by Xie and colleagues.

Similarly, OH was not a focus of the present study, but OH sheds light on COF and its clinical uses and limitations. Like OH, COF involves an insufficient haemodynamic response to orthostatic activity and predicts orthostatic symptoms and increased falls. Our group recently used transthoracic echocardiogram to compare CO in supine and standing positions in an ambulatory population.8 We found that orthostatic changes in CO were driven largely by HR. This finding is consistent with the present study, where COF showed a blunted HR response compared with COR. However, our findings suggest that CO may not be an effective parameter for OH evaluation, because more easily measured vital signs (e.g. HR and BP) provide sufficient data for diagnosis of OH, and clinical correlates (e.g. hypovolaemia, beta-blocker therapy, and evidence of dysautonomia) support diagnosis of the underlying aetiology. To justify the technology and effort involved in its detection, COF will need to demonstrate clinical utility beyond already measurable parameters.

If generalizable and reproducible, the COF phenotype has two principal clinical implications. First, it suggests heterogeneous aetiologies of insufficient haemodynamic responses to standing from the supine position. A second implication is that COF may help identify patients without OH who are at risk of falls. However, clinicians would need to know whom to evaluate for COF. In COF, as in OH, symptoms may be non-specific or completely absent, making it difficult to identify who should be screened. Moreover, unlike OH, most clinics lack the technology to detect COF using the protocols from the present study (e.g. advanced beat-to-beat haemodynamic monitoring). Correlating these findings with practical, measurable clinical signs is critical for real-world practice.

Clinicians will also need to consider how this study relates to their patient populations. The younger, Melbourne cohort included medical students without cardiovascular disease, and the older, TILDA cohort included only Caucasian participants. These results may not be generalizable to older, non-white populations, who often have a higher burden of cardiovascular disease, OH, and falls.2,9,10 In addition, the clustering of demographic characteristics across multiple field sites in the present study raises concerns for ecological bias (e.g. unmeasured geographic differences or non-standardized field centre practices) across sites that could explain population differences beyond known demographic differences such as age.

Although clinical outcomes were included in TILDA, the present study used historic rather than prospective data to examine associations between CO phenotypes and outcomes. This allows for recollection as well as selection bias, as participants who have already fallen may be less likely to return for future study visits. Such bias extends across much cardiovascular research in older adults: those who are most affected by orthostatic intolerance and frailty are often least likely to present for these studies. Researchers will need to find ways to better include frail and house-bound participants in future prospective work.

Xie et al. meaningfully add to the growing recognition that healthy cardiovascular haemodynamics are critical to prevent adverse clinical outcomes such as falls. Their work identifies a novel pathological phenotype of inadequate cardiovascular response to standing among older adults and, with it, potential treatment targets to prevent falls. However, the clinical implications of this phenotype among younger adults remain unclear. Future work should determine who should be screened for COF or similar conditions, which clinical signs might suggest these conditions, and the clinical significance of this phenotype across the life span.

# Ivan Illich and convivial palliative care

Aldis H. Petriceks, M.D., M.P.H.

Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

During my final rotation of medical school, I cared for an older woman with severe aortic stenosis and chronic kidney disease. She was an extremely pleasant woman – kind, thoughtful, grateful – much like her husband and son, who visited daily. But her physiology was tenuous. Too much fluid and her kidneys would lag behind and her lungs fill with water. Too little hydration and her heart would not squeeze enough to replenish vital organs. Each day was a tightrope juggling act of kidney function, cardiac output, hemodynamics, and electrolyte derangements.

After a week of little progress, I organized a family meeting. We spoke for over an hour, describing the fragile physiology that constrained us. The patient drifted in and out of the conversation, her senses dulled by rising uremia. We could try more diuresis, I said, and potentially ease her breathing. We might also cause damage, drying up what little fluid she had remaining. I touched on the possibility that there was no true fix to her problems. But if there was no fix – ?

I told them about hospice and comfort care. We were not there yet. But we could be there shortly. After a long conversation, we decided to try another round of diuresis and watch her kidney function and mental status. It would take a few days to know whether this had worked.

To a certain degree, it did. Her kidney function improved, her cardiac output appeared intact, and she was more alert. This was not a total victory, but her husband and son were grateful. I had only 5 or 6 patients on my list, so I spent hours with them as my rotation wound down. They showed me photos from her youth, told me I was her favorite doctor. The son smiled when I walked in the room. I returned each night after sign-out to answer their questions or call the husband if I hadn’t seen them in the afternoon.

That was the case on my last day. After a warm goodbye with my attending, I went to the patient’s room and found her asleep, by herself, the uremia making her hard to wake, her seesaw physiology swinging back from a brief reprieve. I didn’t want to bother her, so I left a short note to be read when she woke up. This may never have happened. I left the hospital and walked in the warm early-summer air, grabbed my bike, and cycled to my dormitory.

Around this time, I had been reading quite a lot of Ivan Illich, the 20th-century social critic, Catholic priest, university professor, and public intellectual, perhaps most famous (certainly among clinicians) for his 1976 publication, Medical Nemesis, later updated to Limits to Medicine (O’Mahony 2016). Illich was not without his flaws, but he drew me in with his provocative and frankly polemical critiques of the “medical establishment,” which he saw as one of several modern institutions whose activities constituted a “paradoxical counterproductivity” – an active undermining of their original aims (Illich 1976). Among these institutions he also included mass obligatory schooling, modern transport systems, and contemporary modes of energy production and distribution (Illich 1970, 1973, 1974). At the center of Illich’s critique was the idea that human beings had a natural capacity to learn, move, build, heal, and face death, and to do this for themselves and within communities of mutual support and personal interdependence.

What Illich criticized was the increasing tendency to “expropriate” these activities as the products of impersonal institutions. In each of his major works – which exerted great influence at the time, and were reviewed by the likes of the New York Times and New York Review of Books – he questioned not the existence but rather the unquestioned centrality and expansion of hospitals, highways, and school certificates. These things could had their place in society, but their ideal use, in Illich’s view, was not toward constant growth but rather conviviality. He defined this as “individual freedom realized in personal interdependence,” a reciprocal growth in autonomy and community, in which tradition and shared knowledge contributed to each person’s ability to care for themselves and for their neighbor.

One of his favorite parables was that of the Good Samaritan, from the Christian New Testament (Cayley 1992, 2021). In the parable, a man is beaten and left for dead on the side of the road, unaided by passing strangers from his tribe. A man from a rival tribe, the Samaritans, stops and binds his wounds and pays for his recovery in a nearby inn. The Samaritan, as Illich pointed out, is not directed by any ethical imperative – individuals from the two people groups were not expected to assist one another in this way – but rather by compassion, by being “moved in his guts” (Cayley 1992, 2021).

Jesus delivers the parable in the New Testament in response to a question about the imperative to love one’s neighbor as oneself. Who is this neighbor? To whom do we owe this love? The answer is more complicated than the usual interpretation. By assisting a man from an opposing tribe, the logic goes, the Samaritan shows that everyone is the neighbor. But Illich argued that the Samaritan is not obeying any ethical code when he decides to help the man left for dead on the side of the road. He is moved in his guts, gratuitously touched on a physical and emotional level. The man on the road is not an abstraction or an ethical case study, but a human being who has the potential to become the neighbor in the process of mutual care and recognition. The Samaritan has the ability to choose whom he will recognize as a neighbor, in a way that cannot be prescribed by codes or institutions.

It is this spirit of autonomy, interpersonal dependence, and gratuitous generosity that Illich wanted for modern medicine. He claimed that the growth of medicine into a massive industry had interfered with its convivial potential, and that this turned care into a commodity rather than a human activity, a noun rather than a verb (Illich 1973). He was a “proscriptive” rather than a “prescriptive” thinker, as David Cayley argues, and did not devise a detailed solution to this problem. As Lewis Thomas wrote in his review of Medical Nemesis, “it is possible to read the whole book through, nodding much of the time in general agreement,” but another issue arises “when it is finished … and you try to figure out what Illich wants to have done about it” (Thomas 1976).

And yet, despite these limitations, I returned to Illich after saying goodbye to my patient, and I continue to return to him during my internship. I have seen a good deal of pain and death in the last several years, much of which has happened in the hospital and thus within the purview of a massive and highly specialized caregiving institution. Almost all of it has gone far beyond the caregiving capacity of loved ones who must continue to work, raise families, and sleep. Even with the rise of palliative care interest and training, and the consequent attention to goals of care and the avoidance of unnecessary intervention, we therefore retain the possibility of non-convivial care, of delivering a product instead of fostering human activity. We attend closely to patient-centered care, including patients and their families in our decision-making, as I did during the family meeting for my patient. But I wonder what it would have meant to make that care convivial, to help my

patient and their family care for one another, not only to provide care to them. Maybe I achieved this. Maybe partially.

The first time I read Ivan Illich, I mistook his name for a misspelling of Ivan Ilyich, the protagonist of a Tolstoy novella (Tolstoy et al. 2010). Years ago, when I was a hospice volunteer before medical school, I published an article in this journal about that novella (Petriceks 2019). I focused on Gerasim, a young peasant, as perhaps the sole caregiver whom the fictional Ivan Ilyich genuinely appreciates. Gerasim evokes this appreciation through “honesty, authenticity, and humility,” I wrote, and this is true, but as a doctor, I now see Gerasim in a different light. He embodies all those traits, but he is also slow, gracefully limited, equipped with his own physical ability to carry and comfort Ivan Ilyich. There is no abstract professional identity or ethical imperative guiding him. He responds gratuitously to the suffering man who enters his life. He is caring, compassionate.

In a word, convivial.
